s: A healthcare company is designing a patient portal. The portal must use a database to store patient dat a. The portal must encrypt all data at rest and in transit. The portal must audit all data access. Database users must not be able to tamper with the audit trail. The company must retain the audit data for 10 years. The audit data must be immutable. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
o: Store data in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL encrypted database. Enforce the use of TLS for all connections.
Store data in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL encrypted database. Enforce the use of TLS for all connections.
Create a database activity stream in the database cluster. Use Amazon Data Firehose to send the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 10-year retention period.

Install pgAudit in the database cluster. Store the data in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon Data Firehose to send the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 10-year retention period.

Install pgAudit in the database cluster. Store the data in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon Data Firehose to send the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Enable S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 10-year retention period.
e: A and C are correct. Aurora PostgreSQL can store patient data in an encrypted database and can enforce TLS for encrypted connections in transit. For tamper-resistant auditing, Aurora Database Activity Streams are the stronger choice because they monitor database activity and send the stream to Amazon Kinesis for external consumption. AWS documentation states that activity streams monitor and report activities and that the activity stream is collected and transmitted to Kinesis. Sending those audit records to Amazon S3 and enabling S3 Object Lock in compliance mode provides immutable retention. Compliance mode prevents protected object versions from being overwritten or deleted by any user, including the root user, during the retention period. pgAudit logs in CloudWatch are useful, but they do not provide the same database activity stream control and immutability pattern.

w.y: 'Database users must not be able to tamper with the audit trail' points to Database Activity Streams, which push activity outside the database's control and are supported on Aurora PostgreSQL. Delivering to S3 with Object Lock in compliance mode for 10 years makes the records immutable.

o.A: Correct: encrypted Aurora PostgreSQL with forced TLS, which also supports activity streams.
o.B: RDS for PostgreSQL does not support Database Activity Streams.
o.C: Correct: activity stream through Firehose to S3 with compliance-mode Object Lock.
o.D: pgAudit is configured inside the database, so privileged database users can change or turn it off.
o.E: Same pgAudit problem, and governance mode can be overridden by users with special permissions.
